title: Microsoft profits soar days after announcing thousands of layoffs
description: Technology giant Microsoft says its profits for the three months to the end of September jumped to more than $36.6bn (£27.5bn), just days after announ
body: Technology giant Microsoft says its profits for the three months to the end of September jumped to more than $36.6bn (£27.5bn), just days after announcing plans to cut its workforce by more than a quarter.On Monday, the Windows developer said it would offer buyouts to around 60,000 of its workers to cut costs as it pours billions of dollars into artificial intelligence (AI).Like many other major tech firms, Microsoft is investing heavily in the infrastructure that powers AI even as questions remain over whether such huge spending will pay off.Microsoft shares rose by almost 2.9% in after hours trading in New York on Wednesday.The recent financial results of tech companies have been closely watched by investors as they gauge whether the heavy spending on AI is sustainable.Big tech companies like Amazon, Meta and Alphabet are expected to spend more than $700bn this year on AI chips and infrastructure like data centres.Microsoft said on Wednesday that its quarterly revenue rose to $92.3bn - up 19% from a year earlier - driven by strong growth in its cloud computing business.Its earnings were lifted by a 30% increase in revenue for Microsoft Cloud - its range of enterprise technology services.The firm also flagged risks, including "substantial investments" in AI, among other uncertainties that could impact its finances.The firm's chief executive Satya Nadella said AI development has helped grow the adoption of the technology and has delivered "real-world impact across every industry."

schema.headline: Microsoft profits soar days after announcing thousands of layoffs

title: Poundland's future hangs in the balance as chain edges towards collapse
description: The future of Poundland hangs in the balance as the discount chain edges towards collapse, the BBC understands.The retailer has filed a notice of inte
body: The future of Poundland hangs in the balance as the discount chain edges towards collapse, the BBC understands.The retailer has filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which if approved by the High Court, will give the business 10 days breathing space to find a rescue deal.Poundland's managing director Barry Williams wrote a memo to his 12,000 staff across its 600 stores in the UK and Ireland saying the American owner of the chain had limited the chain's access to funding.Gordon Brothers bought Poundland, which had been struggling, from the Polish retail group Pepco last year for a nominal £1.But little over a year later it put the business up for sale in September.Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG) put forward a bid to take the business on as a going concern, but it is understood this did not meet Gordon Brothers' expectations.Gordon Brothers wants to recoup a £30m shareholder loan it inherited from the previous owners as part of a its deal, but it is understood the Martin Property Group offer fell short of that £30m total. It is understood MPG was not prepared to pay the full amount in advance.It means Poundland is now heading towards an insolvency process as Gordon Brothers either secures a new owner through what is known as a pre-pack administration, or it could break the business up and sell parcels of stores to interested parties such as Iceland, Lidl, and B&M.However, there is a split between the owners and the management running Poundland, who described the situation as "unexpected, unwanted and wholly avoidable"."As you all know, our sales are strong and our recovery is taking root. This business simply does not deserve to go into any kind of administration," said Williams, the chain's managing director.He revealed that Gordon Brothers had limited Poundland's access to funds which help it run its day-to-day business in a message to his staff this week."I'm disappointed to have to tell you that Gordon Brothers have given instructions that restricts our access to funds that we would, in normal circumstances expect to access fully under our existing loan agreement," he added.In the memo, seen by the BBC, Williams said the offer from Martin Property Group was a "fully funded, ready to go bid that would have kept the business intact and able to continue the remarkable progress we've made".Three independent directors who were appointed earlier this month to help oversee a sale have resigned with immediate effect after disagreeing with Gordon Brothers' decision not to accept MPG's solvent offer.If its notice to appoint adminstrators is approved, the management team will be given breathing space to look for a rescue deal. The move creates a 10 day pause on creditors calling in debts. Poundland's main creditor is its owner, Gordon Brothers.The BBC understands Gordon Brothers has lined up AlixPartners as administrators.Gordon Brothers has been approached for comment, but in an earlier statement it said while MPG was identified as the "preferred bidder" by Poundland's management team, "attention must now turn to other active bids"."As well as interest from buyers for the whole business, the sale process has also surfaced a number of formal and indicative offers for significant viable parts of the business from established retail operators," they added."These options will now be objectively evaluated, with a view to minimising uncertainty for Poundland's people and all relevant stakeholders."AlixPartners declined to comment.

schema.headline: Poundland's future hangs in the balance as chain edges towards collapse

title: US Health Secretary RFK Jr to expand access to unapproved peptides
description: The peptides mentioned in the plan include BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c and Semax. Compounding pharmacies will be able to mix them to create medicatio
body: The peptides mentioned in the plan include BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c and Semax. Compounding pharmacies will be able to mix them to create medications.The BBC has contacted the FDA for comment.An FDA advisory panel voted in July to loosen restrictions on the six peptides. But FDA staff members recommended against it.Kennedy has described himself as a "big fan" of the drugs and has previously vowed to ease restrictions on them after the Biden administration clamped down on the growing industry.Peptides are short chains of amino acids, or small proteins, which our bodies naturally produce. They act as messengers, telling cells what to do, and play vital roles in skin health, immune system and hormone regulation.Peptides have been used to treat medical conditions for more than a century. Insulin, one of the first peptide hormones to be discovered, helps people with Type 1 diabetes and some with Type 2 manage their blood sugar levels.But now unregulated peptides have exploded onto the wellness market since GLP-1s, weight loss drugs, became mainstream.Online influencers have been marketing peptides in what they have called "stacks" for unproven uses, claiming they can be used as a quick way to help people look younger, heal or improve their skin.They have become popular among teens on TikTok, especially boys, over unproven claims they help to build muscle, part of online trends known as "biohacking" and "looksmaxxing".Health experts have cautioned against use of the drugs, citing a lack of clinical trials for humans and the unknown long-term effects of the substances.

schema.headline: US Health Secretary RFK Jr to expand access to unapproved peptides

title: What the Budget offers for under 25s - and what it leaves out
description: If you are an 18-to-20 year-old earning the minimum wage, your pay will go up by 3.9% from next April.However, the increase may be lower than you had
body: If you are an 18-to-20 year-old earning the minimum wage, your pay will go up by 3.9% from next April.However, the increase may be lower than you had expected. That is because Healey reversed course on how his Labour predecessor, Rachel Reeves, had been increasing the minimum wage for young people. Labour had promised to do away with "discriminatory age bands", with all adults entitled to the same minimum wage. This year, 18-20 year-olds will see the same increase as older workers, meaning the disparity will remain. So, for 18-to-20 year-olds, your pay will rise to £11.27, while over-20s will be paid a minimum of £13.21 an hour.The increase also means a 21-year-old, who is working full time on the minimum wage and took out a student loan after 2023, will now earn enough to meet the £25,000 repayment threshold, over which they will start paying back 9% of their earnings.The Budget contained plans to help people get onto the housing ladder, including the introduction of a "First Time Buyer Isa". This is an account in which savers can build up a deposit, with the government topping up contributions of up to £4,000 each year with a 25% bonus. The new savings account will be introduced in 2029, replacing the existing Lifetime Isa, which has been criticised by some for imposing harsh penalties on those buying homes for more than the £450,000 cap. The cap will remain, but the new "First Time Buyer Isa" will ensure savers are not penalised by losing their own money when making withdrawals. Savers will only lose contributions made by the government when making withdrawals which are not eligible for the account.The penalty for withdrawals from existing Lifetime Isas will be lowered, too, to address concerns about savers being punished.  The government had already revealed a £4.7bn scheme for first-time buyers in England dubbed Your First Home. It is aiming to help 70,000 individuals and couples get on the housing ladderThe scheme will allow people to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It will provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.Capped at £110,000 outside London and £140,000 in the capital, it is aimed at those hoping to get on the housing ladder without help from "the bank of mum and dad".

schema.headline: What the Budget offers for under 25s - and what it leaves out

title: Healey buys himself some time, but big questions unanswered
description: John Healey talked of charting a new course for Britain, but this Budget was more about course-correcting than charging down a new path.It was abundan
body: John Healey talked of charting a new course for Britain, but this Budget was more about course-correcting than charging down a new path.It was abundantly clear that the financial fallout from that conflict in the Middle East has hampered the finances of households and businesses – and the government's ability to help.While the government targeted those impacted by higher energy and fuel bills, the "breathing space" it aimed to provide was limited; it is a pill that doesn't fully alleviate the pain.The most telling evidence was that official forecasters predict that while earnings will rise, that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes. Even after the extra help is taken into account, households' incomes after inflation and tax are set to be typically lower across the next two years than the start of the parliament. On that basis, it could be the second worse parliament for living standards, after the last one, since the 1950s - a sign of how far the war has blown prosperity off course.But it can't be all be blamed on the war. Taxes haven't helped. Although there were few major measures aimed at households, the policy of previous chancellors of freezing the thresholds at which different rates of tax on income apply - fiscal drag - has been maintained in the background, scooping more money out of pay packets.Overall, this Budget has the tax burden - the proportion of the nation's income going to the tax office - rising to a new historic high of 38.6%However, a more generous package of help would have been hard to pull off. The impact of higher inflation and debt have increased borrowing costs by £14bn in the past year alone.The Chancellor had to prove to the markets which lend the government money that he has a plan to bring down future debt to avoid those costs climbing further.As it stands, debt interest repayments are due to be £160bn in 2032, more than double the amount spent on schools in England.And the plans Healey has unveiled already eat into wiggle room he has within the public finances. He says he was right to do so - that's what such safety margins are there for - in times of strife. But the great uncertainty that remains made going further very risky. Energy prices remaining high, for example, could easily chew up all the spare cash.So the result was what some have termed a beige, safe Budget. As Healey strove to prove his fiscally sound credentials, there wasn't even the customary rabbit pulled out of the hat, the end-of-speech sweetener.The markets seem reassured – even if some of his tax raising plans involve clamping down on loopholes and those not paying the right tax, which is always highly uncertain.So the chancellor appears to have bought himself some breathing space. But that means some big questions have been postponed until another day, not least on public services.Higher-than-expected inflation may mean that if areas such as health and defence are prioritised, budgets for some other "unprotected" areas – justice and higher education for example – are set to lag behind inflation after 2028.There was a hint too from John Healey that he'd tap into some of those budgets to help out defence spending. To maintain those budgets in 2030 would means finding tens of billions of pounds.And issues around the other big area of spending – welfare – remain unresolved. Between 2025 and 2032, spending there is set to increase by £100bn.The official forecasters also noted the rapid rise in sickness and disability caseloads since the start of the pandemic. They warn if that trend continued, spending on such benefits would rise by a further £13bn.Any suggestion of welfare reform has been postponed until the forthcoming review into the plight of workless young people.Then there's the issue of boosting growth. There was a bit more detail on the plans for devolution – but there is much to be fleshed out. And on another key part of the growth strategy, housebuilding, there was disappointing news. Even though first-time buyers are set to get more help, their first home may be more elusive.Between regulation and higher costs – in part, related to the war - the OBR estimates that 190,000 fewer homes will be built by 2032 compared to what it thought in March, a significant setback.So the chancellor may have unveiled 98 (relatively small) measures but the to-do list gets longer.With his official forecasters warning that, in a very uncertain world, his finances face exceptional risks, playing a wait-and-see game feels like a prudent move.The risks go both ways: the OBR points out that a swift resolution to the war and an improvement in the economy could spell a significant boost to the public finances.So the chancellor has more reason than most to keep his fingers crossed that happens rapidly.For as it stands, the official forecasters say incomes after inflation, living standards, are set to be only 1% higher at the end of the decade than at the start.A series of economic shocks outside out control could thwart plans to turbo-boost prosperity . And as today shows, breathing space only extends so far.

schema.headline: Healey buys himself some time, but big questions unanswered

title: John Healey promises reduction in welfare bill before next election
description: John Healey has pledged there will be a "reduction in the benefits bill" before the next general election, after opponents criticised his first Budget
body: John Healey has pledged there will be a "reduction in the benefits bill" before the next general election, after opponents criticised his first Budget for lacking details on welfare reform.The chancellor told the BBC it is "simply not good for Britain or progressive to have a bigger and bigger benefits bill", labelling the current system "unsustainable". He ruled out "crude cuts" but more details on his approach are not expected until two major reviews are published next month.The Conservatives accused Labour of being "addicted to welfare", while Reform UK said the Budget did not address the "ballooning" benefits bill. Welfare spending is forecast to rise this year by £19bn to £353bn.Watchdog and forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said this figure is expected to rise to £431bn in 2031/32, driven primarily by health-related and pensioner benefit spending.The government has already pledged to reform the existing state pension triple lock from 2030, and more proposals and changes to the welfare system are expected to emerge in the coming months. Healey told MPs that a review of disability benefits co-chaired by Labour minister Sir Stephen Timms and one on young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) led by former minister Alan Milburn will be published in November.The government is then expected to respond by the end of the year and publish a policy document setting out proposals, and legislation next year. Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme in the hours after the Budget, Healey said the government had a "moral duty" to help the almost one million young people out of work, education or training.The chancellor added that giving them the opportunity to "fulfil their potential" and contribute to the economy can help the government "bring the welfare bill down in the long-term".Pressed on whether there will be cuts in welfare spending before the election, Healey replied: "There will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we'll do that in a Labour way and we'll do that because it is simply not good for Britain or progressive to have a bigger and bigger benefits bill."The chancellor's remarks came after Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch responded to the Budget by saying the benefits bill was "going up by tens of billions of pounds because this government has put welfare first".She said the country was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed, and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system", adding that the Budget was "not bold enough".Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said welfare reform "needs to be done right", adding this should involve "cutting the bill by helping people into work and giving people the care and support they need so that they can work".Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, noted the government still has "many difficult decisions" to take after not fleshing out several big issues, including disability benefits and support for young people.Conservative MP and former chancellor Sir Jeremy Hunt said one of the key rules was to "never waste a Budget", adding that Healey could have explained how he would get hundreds of thousands of young people "off welfare and into work".After highlighting other policy areas not detailed in the Budget, Sir Jeremy told the House of Commons: "I fear that the chancellor and the prime minister have wasted the political capital that they have by putting off difficult decisions."He added: "The problem is these decisions are going to be harder in a year's time than they are today."One area where Healey did make announcements in the Budget was on energy prices.Millions of households will get £100 to help with soaring energy bills to be paid for by a tax on bank profits, which Healey said would give "breathing space now" to people.The one-off payment will be given to people living in council tax bands A to D in England, with Wales saying it will match the payment and the Scottish government planning to "replicate" it.Gas standing charges in England, Scotland and Wales are also to be scrapped during 2027 "or as soon as possible after". These fixed daily fees will be shifted onto the price of each unit of energy, meaning heavy gas users will face higher bills.Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Healey was pressed over warnings that the £100 energy bill support would not be enough as forecasts suggest an annual bill could increase by a far greater amount from January.Healey said: "There are experts who say at least this is going to help people get through the winter."There's no way, if I'm honest with people and I want to be, that government can make payments that are going to remove all these price pressures that are driven by the war in the Middle East."For the Green Party, Ellie Chowns described the Budget as having "failed to engage with the real issues facing our country", and Reform's Robert Jenrick said it was an "exercise in fiddling while the economy burns".

schema.headline: John Healey promises reduction in welfare bill before next election

title: Carney to push for closer ties at Canada-EU summit in Montreal
description: For decades, Canada-EU summits took place without much fanfare - but that's not the case for this coming two-day meeting in Montreal. Thursday and Fri
body: For decades, Canada-EU summits took place without much fanfare - but that's not the case for this coming two-day meeting in Montreal. Thursday and Friday's summit will be closely watched for details on how Canada  and the European bloc deepen their ties.Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed "opening the door" to Canada for what she called an "associate membership" - a status that does not currently exist.The overture came after Prime Minister Carney addressed the European Parliament in Strasbourg, telling EU lawmakers that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".Carney and many EU member states welcome closer ties, but not all are on board with what to call this new relationship. Some, like Germany, are questioning the "associate member" term, fearing that Canada is getting preferential treatment ahead of other nations who also want in.According to reports by multiple news outlets, Germany and other nations successfully lobbied to remove mention of the title in a draft statement ahead of the summit, opting instead for softer language that references an "ever closer association".Germany's ambassador to Canada, Matthias Lüttenberg, told CTV News on Tuesday that some member states were "a little surprised" by von der Leyen's announcement. The concept of "associate membership", he added, is something that is not clearly understood as it pertains to Canada."Germany has been using the term of associate membership for something completely different, which is the relationship of the EU to Ukraine and potentially Moldova", he said, both of which have been trying to join the bloc for many years.Lüttenberg noted, however, that neither Canada nor the EU is seeking full membership for the North American country.Rather, both want to bring Canada "as close as possible" to the bloc without membership.On the first day of the summit, Carney and von der Leyen and business leaders from both Europe and Canada will gather for a business forum.Canadian officials said they also expect agreements to be hammered out on defence, critical minerals, research and trade over the two days. Speaking to reporters earlier this week, European officials downplayed the possibility of a major announcement on Canada's new relationship with EU, saying much will be sorted in the coming months. But both Canadian and EU officials have provided some clues on what the relationship could look like, including closer business ties and allowing more students to study on either side of the Atlantic. Canada also does not plan on paying a membership fee similar to other EU nations, Canadian officials have said. Instead, it is looking at participating in different EU programmes that would benefit both Canada and member states.And despite some disagreement about the wording, both have signalled they are fully on board with deepening ties."The wording is emblematic of the ambition," said one senior Canadian official who was granted anonymity to speak to reporters at a briefing ahead of the summit. Since taking office last year, Prime Minister Carney has pushed Canada closer to Europe as his country continues to deal with an ongoing trade war with the US, its neighbour and largest trading customer. US President Donald Trump has called the idea of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU "laughable", and has threatened "very serious tariffs" on Europe if he considered it a "hostile act".Canadian officials stressed on Wednesday that their pivot to Europe is not meant to offend anybody, but rather to build on work that was already underway. Canada recently signed an agreement that gives its defence companies procurement access to the EU's Security and Defence Partnership programme. It also signed a landmark energy deal with Germany in May that would see the first-ever long-term shipments of liquified natural gas from Canada to Europe in the coming years.Carney said earlier this week that the summit would "launch further formal discussions" between Canada and the EU on deepening ties and creating new opportunities for both sides.As for what this new relationship status will be called, the prime minister said the "nomenclature" does not matter. "What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians," he said.

schema.headline: Carney to push for closer ties at Canada-EU summit in Montreal

title: Details of thousands of US immigration agents leaked in major hack
description: Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcemen
body: Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcement, have been leaked to the public.The leak includes names, work addresses and phone numbers of DHS staff, including agents working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection, along with descriptions of the work they do for each agency.Wednesday's leak marks the third time in recent weeks that a government agency has been targeted by leaks or hacks.A DHS spokesperson said the agency is "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.""We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected," the spokesperson added. "We will update the public when more information is available."The seemingly unprecedented breach of employee information was made public online. A group called the Department of Peace accessed the information from DHS, while journalist and cybersecurity researcher maia crimew alongside the website Distributed Denial of Secrets put it online.The information was put in a database named Icepick.Most of the agents included, more than 21,000 of them, work for CBP, according to the data. Nearly 6,600 work for ICE. Other records show agents with Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Protective Service and even people working for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.The leaked information also included dozens of previously unknown operation names, the agents that led and worked on those operations, and some of the technology they used in their work, including tech provided by Cellbrite and Palantir.   The groups wrote in an online statement that the the leak was not meant to be a directory of every DHS agent. Rather the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability", according to Emma Best, a co founder of DDoSecrets."The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in its simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation - along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," Best added.BlueLeaks refers to a massive leak of US police data in 2020, data from which DDoSecrets also hosted.A spokesperson for the Department of Peace pointed directly at actions by ICE agents for the group's work to hack DHS records. "On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat'. This is what happens to ICE when you do that," the spokesperson wrote on Wednesday.Mullin in March became Secretary of Homeland Security. The Department of Peace said it accessed the DHS agent profiles through a single sign-on service called Okta.Okta is a popular online security tool that organisations use to ensure that only people with access to internal platforms are logging on to them.A spokeswoman for Okta said the company is aware of the claims being made, but said: "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised."Last month, the FBI was hacked by a group called ShinyHunters, which took personal information about thousands of agents. In recent days, the Federal Election Commission, which makes public political campaign donation data, was taken offline because of a suspected hacking attempt. Public backlash to US immigration enforcement has been building as the Trump Administration has pushed a huge increase in arrests and deportations of people suspected of being in the country illegally.Immigration operations this year have repeatedly turned violent, external, with ICE agents shooting at more than two dozen people and killing at least nine people. Those killings include the high profile deaths of Alex Pretti and Renee Good, both of whom were shot and killed by ICE agents this year in Minnesota, despite not being the targets of arrests.Often, ICE agents carry out enforcement actions while their faces are covered by masks and sunglasses. Immigration agents rarely identify themselves, despite being required by law to do so, and US politicians have publicly demanded, external DHS enforces the requirement. Since President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025, the US has enacted nearly 1 million deportations, external, according to data from the Migration Policy Institute. More than 70% of the deportations have been of people with no criminal record.

schema.headline: Details of thousands of US immigration agents leaked in major hack

title: George Michael: Row over dozens items up for auction
description: A family row has broken out over an auction of George Michael memorabilia taking place on Thursday.The guitar the singer-songwriter performed with in
body: A family row has broken out over an auction of George Michael memorabilia taking place on Thursday.The guitar the singer-songwriter performed with in the Faith music video is one of several items being auctioned by Sworders from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, Michael's long-time personal assistant.  Siobhan died in 2014 and the items are being sold by her estranged husband Ian Belcher, who inherited them after her death.Gerard Bailey, Siobhan's brother, told the BBC she "would be horrified at the prospect of the auction being held in her name and that her personal, cherished possessions are being sold off to the highest bidder". Both Sworders and Belcher declined to comment.Sworders describes the 32 lots as a "remarkable group of memorabilia from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, George Michael's long-time personal assistant and trusted confidante".Michael grew up in Hertfordshire and shot to fame alongside Andrew Ridgeley in pop duo Wham! He went on to enjoy solo success with hits such as Faith, Careless Whisper, Father Figure, Outside and Fastlove. He died in 2016.Siobhan was in the process of divorcing Belcher when she died, but was legally still married to him. She did not leave a will. Her brother claimed she had started to draw up a will shortly before she died, which would have left the items to her nieces and nephews, but it was not registered.There is no suggestion that Belcher does not have the right to sell the items, because her estate legally passed to him when she died.Bailey said if his sister had lived a few weeks longer, the items would not have passed to Belcher because he would not have been considered her next of kin. In a letter to the auction house seen by the BBC, Bailey said the rest of the family considers the auction a "breach of [Siobhan's] privacy", adding that the use of her name is "disingenuous" and "wholly unethical".He told the auction house that Belcher's "misuse of my sister's name" is "frankly dishonourable", and profiteering from the items was "egregiously shameful".Bailey has asked that the auction should not go ahead, or, if it does, that it be in Belcher's name rather than Siobhan's.Bailey began working as Michael's personal assistant in 1984, joining him in the year Wham! had their first number-one hit with Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go.She remained his PA for 20 years, and her brother told BBC News she avoided the limelight and guarded the pop star's privacy, despite the attention of tabloid journalists hoping for stories."I think she was one of the few people George trusted and whose opinion he valued," Bailey said."She was always honest and straight with him. I guess that's why she stayed working for him for so long through the very, very good and not so good times."The guitar now going under the hammer was "a gift" to his sister because the singer "thought so much of her", he said.The instrument had a key role to play in Michael's reinvention from teen pop idol to serious solo artist.In the 1987 video for Faith, Michael - in ripped blue Levi's jeans, white T-shirt and black leather biker jacket - strummed the vintage acoustic guitar that he reportedly picked up in a shop in Los Angeles shortly beforehand.Guitarist magazine recently billed it as "arguably the most famous Gretsch Synchromatic in the world".It has an estimated price tag of between £60,000 and £120,000. Other less significant but more personal items have already exceeded their estimates.A Filofax from the 1988 Faith tour with Siobhan's handwritten notes and annotations had a guide price of up to £600 and a current bid of £1,750.Other items include a note written "with love and admiration" from Michael and Ridgeley, an official Wham! photograph signed "To Siobhan (Special...)", and an invitation to Ridgeley's 21st birthday party.The auction also includes the gold disc and platinum CD presented to her for sales milestones achieved by Michael's music."I know she was proud of the various personalised gold and platinum discs she got, though she was very modest about it all," Bailey said.He said "she would never have consented" to the sale of these items, adding that the auction "breaks my heart"."I think she'd be devastated that something as personal as her Filofax and notes from George are up for grabs. It's just so tawdry and contrary to how she was," he said.Siobhan died suddenly and unexpectedly of natural causes at the age of 56. According to her brother, she wanted the possessions to "have remained with her family and we would never have sold".He accused Belcher of deciding "12 years after my sister's death to cash in".Bailey acknowledged that Belcher has a legal right to sell the items but called it "disingenuous" that the sale was being promoted in her name.

schema.headline: George Michael: Row over dozens items up for auction

title: Neighbours: AI micro-drama recut of Australian show focusing on Margot Robbie worries actors and crew
description: Former Neighbours actors and crew have raised concerns about plans to use AI to help re-edit old footage and make mini episodes for mobile phone viewe
body: Former Neighbours actors and crew have raised concerns about plans to use AI to help re-edit old footage and make mini episodes for mobile phone viewers.Fremantle, producer of the now-defunct Australian TV soap opera, has partnered with US-based RoseBerry Media for the project that will use AI to "scan decades of episodes" to help make short vertical videos.Footage of Margot Robbie, who played Donna Freedman from 2008 to 2011, will be the initial focus of the micro-drama.Both companies say the move will bring the show - which aired its final episode last year - to new audiences. But some actors and crew say they have not consented to their images, voice or work to be re-purposed. Robbie has yet to respond publicly. The BBC has contacted her agency for comment.In a statement, the companies behind the project said the AI-assisted technology will "scan decades of episodes to map character arcs, storylines and standout moments, helping editors quickly identify the strongest material".The micro-drama episodes will use "original, previously broadcast footage, dialogue and performances", according to Fremantle spokesman."It does not generate new scenes or performances, alter actors' faces or likenesses, or use synthetic voices," he said, adding that a human editor would be "reviewing and approving every stage of the editing process".The mini episodes will likely feature Matt Werkmeister, 34, who joined the set of Neighbours in 2005 when he was 13 years old. He played a regular character, Zeke Kinski and shared many scenes with Robbie's character.Now a Melbourne-based producer and director, Werkmeister says he hasn't been approached by the companies behind the micro-drama and is concerned what the episodes will feature."If they're creating a new micro-drama out of something that already exists, I feel there needs to be consent for using our image and voice as well as the writers," he said.Robbie is "obviously a big draw card" and "it's nice to watch old clips from shows you used to watch," Werkmeister said, but when he signed his contract two decades ago, "streaming didn't even exist as a platform" so he's unsure of what his rights are.That uncertainty is also at the forefront of Sam Clark's mind. He played Ringo Brown on Neighbours from 2006 to 2010, a character who later marries Robbie's fictional character.Speaking from Los Angeles, Clark – now working as a producer and voice actor - said he hadn't heard about the micro-drama until a friend sent him an article."I don't have a negative view of the work that we did all those years ago getting a second life as long as it's not being manipulated into new storylines," Clark, 39, said."AI and social media obviously wasn't a thing when I signed my contract 20 years ago so I'm still trying to understand exactly what those parameters are."Sound recordist Bruce Findlay, 68, has worked in the TV industry for close to five decades and Neighbours has a "special place" in his heart, having worked on the show from episode one.Using AI to help make short episodes from old footage was "like cutting up a Picasso and rebuilding it"."We worked so hard to get this product out… and now they're chopping it up into little tiny pieces, throwing it up in the air and putting it back together again using AI - it belittles the process".Guy Hameiri, head of RoseBerry Media, said the project is the first time the company will use its in-house AI tool to sift through Neighbours footage - there are more than 9,300 episodes - to make "premium vertical television".The project will "reimagine" the material, giving it "new audiences, new relevance and new value," he said.The head of Fremantle's commercial and international arm, Jens Richter, has called the project "an exciting example of how technology and creative thinking can unlock new value" from their catalogue.It's understood that Fremantle is in discussions with two unions on the issue and that residuals - ongoing payments for actors and writers when their work is re-aired or syndicated - will be paid, but this does not apply to crew.The Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance, one of the unions, confirmed the talks."Workers should be consulted before their likeness or expertise is used in a way they could never had envisioned when they signed contracts decades ago," said MEAA's acting CEO Adam Portelli.

schema.headline: Neighbours: AI micro-drama recut of Australian show focusing on Margot Robbie worries actors and crew

title: Israel's election deadlock is a sign of the country's deep divisions
description: "Democracy is the worst form of government except for all those other forms that have been tried." So said Winston Churchill in the House of Commons i
body: "Democracy is the worst form of government except for all those other forms that have been tried." So said Winston Churchill in the House of Commons in 1947.His aphorism came to mind as Israel's election results filtered through on Tuesday night - exit polls blending with ballots that were cast to dash or fulfil people's hopes and fears.This election has, in some ways, been a celebration of democracy. Voters turning out in record numbers, Jews and Arabs alike. Many spent thousands to fly in from abroad to cast their ballot.At polling stations across the country, we saw the passion of campaigners, as they used every minute to try to change that last mind and win that last vote.President Isaac Herzog said the election was a "badge of honour" for Israeli society. "It is remarkable to see how deep the desire for democracy is in Israel," he exclaimed.Yet this election left the most established democracy in the Middle East without a clear path to a new government. It produced an inconclusive result where neither opposing bloc will have a majority in parliament.Some might say this was business as usual. Israel has never had a one-party government. Its fragmented, proportional representation system is almost designed to govern by coalition.Yet many commentators warned this election had revealed the fundamental and perhaps growing divisions that scar this nation. This was not a plebiscite in which an electorate united around a single cause.How these vastly diverging views coalesce into some form of government is now the unenviable task facing Israel's body politic - the choices and compromises they may have to make could involve fundamental decisions about the country's future.Would Netanyahu be ready to abandon his religious allies and form a coalition with right-wingers from the opposition bloc? Would they be ready to swallow their hostility towards the prime minister and sit in his government?Is the opposition bloc ready to abandon much of its campaign promises and co-operate with Arab parties to force Netanyahu out of office? Are the Arab parties ready to risk joining a government that could fall within months?Yair Golan, the left-wing Democrat leader, urged the opposition bloc to form a partnership with Arab parties. "We must no longer accept Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said.But are the people of Israel ready for such a reality? Amit Segal, an Israeli commentator sympathetic towards Netanyahu, said the high turnout among Arab Israeli voters "reminded Jews on both sides that, after years of division, they may have to learn to sit together after all".The risk is that this election, instead of putting Israel on a new path, has instead raised further doubts about what it is that unites its citizens. What are the common factors that bind this complex, varied collection of peoples into one polity?Autocratic governments, which are growing in number, have long criticised democracies for producing weak and temporary governments, often fragile coalitions that struggle to hold together, let alone deliver what the people wanted.Israel may now struggle for months to form a government. It might even fail and have to hold another election. President Herzog acknowledged this risk head on as he prepared to open coalition negotiations: "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections."For years, Israel has focused on defending itself against its external enemies. But must it also now be ready to defend itself from perils within, if the divisions writ large by this election become unmanageable?In another speech, Churchill once said democracy was not just "insurance against dangers from abroad". It was also, he added, "insurance against dangers scarcely less grave and much more near and constant which threaten us here at home".Can Israel's democracy live up to this challenge?

schema.headline: Israel's election deadlock is a sign of the country's deep divisions

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Healey offers cold comfort' and 'A £100 trick or treat?'
description: Chancellor John Healey is on all of the front pages. Both the Financial Times and the Times describe his Budget as "modest", external. A senior gover
body: Chancellor John Healey is on all of the front pages. Both the Financial Times and the Times describe his Budget as "modest", external. A senior government figure told the FT the Budget was "not radical, but we don't think the markets would have worn something bigger". Similarly, the Guardian says Healey delivered "a low key speech, external designed with febrile bond markets in mind".There's a harsher verdict in the Daily Mail. It says the Budget was "a snoozer", external. In an editorial the paper says that instead of being a blueprint for national renewal the Budget was a holding statement, putting off every major decision facing the country.The Daily Telegraph, external and the Sun say Healey has raised taxes on banks, savers, and landlords, while failing to tackle Britain's ballooning welfare bill. "All the chancellor had to offer was the sound of the cans being kicked down the road," is the Sun's verdict., externalOn its front page the Daily Express highlights the Conservative leader, external, Kemi Badenoch's assessment that the Budget was "not bold enough." The paper has also spoken to the former Tory defence secretary, Sir Ben Wallace, who accuses Healey of putting "benefits before bullets".There's a more positive assessment from the Daily Mirror, external, which titles its coverage "For the Many, Not the Few". The paper says Healey has unveiled a raft of measures to help cash-strapped families and struggling companies. However the Mirror's columnist, Kevin Maguire, asks if the chancellor could have been braver and more radical, with a bigger tax raid on the banks and oil and gas companies.The Guardian is one of the papers highlighting Nigel Farage's claim that he was absent from the Commons on Budget day to avoid a "physical altercation" with another MP in a row about seating arrangements. Farage said a green paper slip, saving him a seat, had been removed. The Guardian says that's because the slip wasn't properly stamped with the date.And the Mirror reports that a grandmother's jewellery collection, discovered in a dusty attic during a house clearance, has sold at auction for more than £500,000. The hoard, found in the town of Malvern in Worcestershire, included pieces from the 19th century through to modern times.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Healey offers cold comfort' and 'A £100 trick or treat?'

title: World Series 2026: Milwaukee Brewers beat Tampa Bay Rays to become MLB champions
description: The Milwaukee Brewers have won the World Series for the first time in the franchise's 57-year history.They beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in game five in
body: The Milwaukee Brewers have won the World Series for the first time in the franchise's 57-year history.They beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in game five in Florida on Wednesday to clinch a 4-1 win in the best-of-seven Fall Classic.The Brewers, whose only previous appearance in the World Series came in 1982, are based in Major League Baseball's smallest market and this year had the 19th highest payroll of its 30 teams.But for the second straight year, the Brewers finished the regular season with MLB's best record and they then proved their class with a dominant run in the play-offs.They avenged last season's loss to the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series by sweeping the two-time defending champions.That secured a spot in the 123rd World Series, where the Brewers became MLB champions with 11 wins from 13 games in the postseason.Milwaukee's William Contreras was named the World Series' most valuable player, with the 28-year-old becoming the eighth catcher to win the award and the third Venezuelan.The Brewers won the first two games in Wisconsin and then the first in Florida, before the Rays, who were the American League's top seed, took it to game five.Milwaukee went ahead at the top of the second inning as a single from Cooper Pratt sent Brice Turang home, before they added another run in the fifth off a David Hamilton hit.The Brewers doubled their lead in their next at-bat through a double from Contreras and Pratt's sacrifice fly.Milwaukee starting pitcher Jacob Misiorowski left the game in the sixth inning and the Rays finally got on the scoreboard in the ninth as Chandler Simpson sent Liam Hicks home off a double.The Brewers entered MLB in 1969 as the Seattle Pilots, but the franchise moved to Milwaukee after only one season.

schema.headline: World Series 2026: Milwaukee Brewers beat Tampa Bay Rays to become MLB champions

title: 'I live with a ghost' - inside the haunted homes attracting bargain hunters
description: From the moment Ryua first walked into her rental apartment in Tokyo she believed it to be haunted."When I visited the place for a viewing there was a
body: From the moment Ryua first walked into her rental apartment in Tokyo she believed it to be haunted."When I visited the place for a viewing there was a man standing there, glaring at me," she says."Since the estate agent couldn't see him, I realised he must be a ghost."While someone more squeamish would probably have quickly left the flat never to return, Ryua chose to go ahead and move in."I'm a bit of a contrarian, so I decided I wanted to become friends with this glaring male ghost," adds Ryua, who works as an aidoru, a young entertainer, and who doesn't wish to share her surname.Four years later, and still in the same apartment, she says she continues to experience paranormal activity on a daily basis. She says she hears endless footsteps and the ghost talking.Although Japan has increasingly marked Halloween, external in recent years, many Japanese people take ghosts seriously all year round. The country has a word, "yuurei", which means a lingering, troubled spirit.These are the ghosts of people who died in violent or tragic circumstances - those who were murdered, killed themselves, or simply were lonely and died alone. If they died at home, then the belief is that their yuurei won't go away.For house hunters who are not superstitious or squeamish it means there are big bargains to be found. There is a whole category of dwellings called jiko bukken, which means "stigmatised" or "incident" properties.Under guidelines issued by the government in 2021, Japanese estate agents must disclose suicide, murder, death by fire, and any death where the body was not discovered for an extended period of time.For rental properties this information must be disclosed for three years, and it must be revealed indefinitely for any property offered for sale.By contrast, in the UK there is no legal requirement, external to reveal that a person died in a property. And in the US, it differs from state to state., external For example, in California you have to reveal if a person has died in the property in the past three years, while in Arizona and Oregon you do not.Ryua was told that a man had killed himself in her apartment. It meant that she gets an almost 30% discount on her rent on her tiny, 25 sq m bedsit in the fashionable ward of Setagaya. She says she pays 45,000 yen ($285; £213) a month, instead of what should have been 62,000 yen.While a house where there had been a murder or suicide would probably be harder to sell or rent out anywhere in the world, Tokyo estate agent Erik Oskamp says that Japanese people are particularly superstitious and averse to stigmatised properties."[Even] an apartment next to a cemetery will be difficult to rent out, especially if you can see the tombs from the kitchen," explains Oskamp. "The worst thing is if a suicide has happened in the apartment. Even if somebody has jumped from the roof, many renters will move out. Other issues are a serious crime or a lonely death."The latter issue, that of a person dying alone, would not generally affect the price of a property in, say, the UK or the US. But in rural Kagoshima, in Japan's southwest, it enabled Diane Tincher to buy a large three-bedroom house for about half of what would have otherwise been the asking price.

schema.headline: 'I live with a ghost' - inside the haunted homes attracting bargain hunters

title: Flávio Bolsonaro denies fleeing Brazil after landing in Miami
description: Bolsonaro's arrival in Florida ended days of confusion over his whereabouts, after he was reported to have travelled to Argentina, and then prematurel
body: Bolsonaro's arrival in Florida ended days of confusion over his whereabouts, after he was reported to have travelled to Argentina, and then prematurely reported to have already entered the US on Tuesday.In a statement, Bolsonaro thanked both the presidents of Argentina and the US, and the American public "who share the same values ​​as the good people of my own country"."It was never my intention to leave my homeland, but I know exactly where this is heading," he said. "I departed from a regime of exception so that I could become the leader my people deserve." He called himself a victim of a coup d'état and political persecution, and said his travel to the US was to protect his family. In the lengthy letter, he also repeated unsubstantiated allegations of "electoral fraud" which he said allowed a "mathematical impossibility" to occur in the election.On Wednesday, Trump declined to discuss the allegations made in Bolsonaro's letter."I won't get involved. It was a very strange election, that's for sure," Trump said. He went on to add that he thought Bolsonaro "and his family were treated very unfairly".After Bolsonaro won the first round of Brazil's election, Lula won the second round by more than four million votes, which was attributed to significantly higher turnout, and swaying more undecided voters.The result was confirmed by the president of Brazil's top electoral court, who was appointed by Bolsonaro's father, former president Jair Bolsonaro. Speculation about Bolsonaro's whereabouts was first triggered by a report on an Argentine news site, which claimed that he had crossed the land border between Brazil and Argentina and then boarded a private plane en route to the US.Brazilian police took the rumours seriously. Early on Tuesday, they checked border crossings but found no evidence that Bolsonaro had left the country, and Argentine officials said they had no reports of him crossing.For a little while, it seemed like Bolsonaro may just be keeping an uncharacteristically low-profile after being unexpectedly beaten by his left-wing rival in the presidential run-off vote on Sunday, in addition to a criminal investigation that led to orders that his passports be turned into authorities. But when he failed to surrender his passports in time to meet a 24-hour deadline on Tuesday, Brazilian authorities cancelled the documents and ordered police to make checks at border posts.Speculation quickly grew that he'd left the country and Bolsonaro's lawyers said they had no idea where he was. But later, however, Argentine migration authorities posted on social media saying that Bolsonaro, his wife, and two daughters had only just crossed into Argentina over land on Tuesday night local time.Flight tracking data verified by the BBC suggested the Bolsonaros departed from Puerto Iguazú in Argentina at 00:18 local time (03:18 GMT) on Wednesday to head to Guayaquil in Ecuador.After a brief stop, the same private jet took them to Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport, where they were pictured disembarking just before 09:30 local time (13:30 GMT).Photographers, who had been waiting for his arrival to finally put an end to all the speculation, swarmed around Bolsonaro as he left the airport in Miami, while his team tried to cover him with umbrellas.Later, Eduardo Bolsonaro posted a photo with his brother Flávio on social media, with the location listed as "United States".The caption read: "Today's photo after reuniting with my brother Flavio Bolsonaro. Yesterday was a long day, perhaps the longest of my life. But we prevailed. Even here outside, we will not give up on Brazil."Flávio Bolsonaro is not the first member of his family to travel to the United States.His father, Jair Bolsonaro, also left Brazil for Florida in December 2022 before his successor, Lula, was inaugurated.Jair was still in the US when his supporters stormed Brazil's government buildings and Supreme Court on 8 January. He later used his absence as part of his defence in his coup trial, which ultimately led to his conviction and 27-year sentence.Flávio's brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, meanwhile, has been living in Texas after taking leave from Brazil's Congress. While in the US, he lobbied officials there in an attempt to influence the coup trial of his father, which led to the US imposing punitive tariffs on Brazil and sanctions on key officials.Eduardo was convicted in absentia over this by Brazil's highest court earlier this year. It is not yet clear what Flávio Bolsonaro's ultimate destination will be, nor how long he plans to stay in the US.He is the subject of two investigations currently pending before Brazil's Supreme Federal Court.One is regarding possible irregularities in the transfer of nearly $70m (£53m) from private bank Banco Master to the film Dark Horse – a biopic about his father.The second investigation relates to alleged money laundering, both of which Bolsonaro denies.He is set to lose his parliamentary immunity on 31 January, when his eight-year Senate term ends.

schema.headline: Flávio Bolsonaro denies fleeing Brazil after landing in Miami
